comments.author: @Urgelt
comments.text:
Excellent reporting, Wes.

For context: the Ottoman Empire held a critical geopolitical advantage: control of trade routes to the far East. That produced enormous wealth - until Spain and Portugal, and then the Dutch, France and especially Great Britain, solved open ocean navigation. That shifted wealth generation away from the Ottomans. Ships could carry larger cargoes than carts.

Refusing to permit printing presses played a very minor role in the shifting geopolitical reality.

But it was tech advances that did the damage.

Tech advances do threaten jobs - never moreso than generative AI. Incumbents in countless fields are certain to try to protect their sinecures.

Autonomous vehicles will throw millions of taxi and truck drivers out of work. The entertainment industry is similarly threatened. Factory jobs. Mining. Refining. Programming. Games production. More.

We don't have an economic model for coping with these disruptions.

I don't think we can stop it. Nor should we. But we do need to figure out how to create and distribute wealth in this new tech age that is being born, so that the advantages are positive for most humans.

It disturbs me that most economists seem to be clueless.

comments.text:
As a filmmaker and 3d artist, I'm super excited for this tech. It will allow me to do so much more, for much less money. And yes, it's hard to produce a film, and bring on appropriate safe investors (I'm burnt on it frankly). This kind of tech, could allow myself and many other filmmakers the opportunity to get what's in our head out there. Maybe a project or set of projects will stand out and shine for many broke filmmakers and artists--and then maybe this will create growth for good people. Listen, I personally have my ten thousand hours in on all the creative apps I've learned through the decades--I plan to flourish with this coming freedom. I'm not going to stop 3d modeling, or stop making films. I'm not going to climb a mountain and scream how angry I am the computer is better than me. I'm going to jump in and get crazy.

Finally, I don't think AI art is stealing. That's ridiculous. That's like telling an artist in school to never mimic another artist. I do believe there are some famous quotes out there that say to do the exact opposite. We as humans learn and mimic. I've been using AI for a few years now, and I have to say, I believe the art I'm creating is far too transformative for artists to get butt hurt over. I'm sorry. We have to adapt. Why not have fun doing it. This isn't going away. I think the way to solve this is to hand out a small portion of money to every artist that was used to train with--if you have two pieces of art up, you won't see much, but if you have hundreds, you may see a decent check. I'm cool with that. Solved.

The web is replete with debates about which of the various image creators makes the best art. The same people will also tell you that these AI's perfectly express the creative intent of their users. But- if it's true that these AI's differ in ways that can be identified and debated- then what they make is not what their users intend but a product of their own internal processes. So the notion that 'human creativity' is being expressed here is a bit of a delusion. At best the human input acts as a seed from which the AI grows it's images, images that are apparantly charecteristic enough to be recognised and debated as the products of that specific AI.

These AI's are incredible inventions but are really one trick ponies in terms of 'creativity'- and the trick is very impressive at first. It works like this; recombine things in novel and striking ways- mix a fox with a crow- or make a tortoise out of glass, or blend a man with a balloon, or combine a hermit crab with a light bulb.. At first sight there seems to be boundless possibilities here, but the more examples I see of 'creative AI' the more I realise that it's just variations of this same trick- recombine things in novel and striking ways.

And these recombinations are fascinating and engaging enough- but can this really be described as creativity? In truth this recombination trick is simply a consequnce of how image generators work, how they turn visual training data into fungible 'raw material' that can then be recombined in an endless number of ways. How long before the novelty of this one trick wears off?

The problem is that true creativity is about having something to say, something to express. And I don't think that when Sora combines a cat with an eel that it is attempting to communicate with us. But- I hear you say- it was the user who 'expressed his creativity' by asking for that eelcat, or that 'horsefly'. But if I gave you a whistle that produced only a single note, what kind of music would you produce with it? creating visual puns via a machine that is uniquely equipped to do just that is hardly a soaring example of human creative expression.
